First results · actual viewing histories

Can Dossier learn from actual film ratings?

We hide films that real viewers rated, give Dossier a few of their other ratings, and check whether it recommends the hidden likes ahead of dislikes.

Anonymous viewers31

Read this first · one minute

What changed when the films were real

This test uses real film descriptions and ratings that viewers gave independently of Dossier. It checks the current model against simple ways to rank the same hidden films.

Learning is weak and uneven

Dossier’s ordering score rises from 53.2% after one rating to 62.0% after 40. A 50% score is chance; higher is better. 21 of 31 viewers have at least one rating order where more evidence makes the score worse. Cutting 20 ratings to five left the score almost unchanged or improved it for 18 viewers.

A simple method wins

After 20 ratings, Dossier scores 61.1%. Public film rating scores 82.3%: a 21.2-point gap for the simple method. At least one simple method beats Dossier for 29 of 31 viewers. Other viewers’ ratings score 82.1%, but they provide extra information.

What people would see

About 4.6 of Dossier’s first ten films are clear likes. The public-rating method finds 6.5. 35.7% of the hidden candidate films are clear likes, so the comparison has room to improve.

Claims improve; questions do not clearly help

Dossier corrected 26 of 28 deliberately selected wrong claims. Its chosen questions changed the 20-rating ordering score by −0.2 points compared with random reasonable films. The difference varies widely across viewers.

Decision: The current recommender needs work before we can claim it learns real viewing histories well. This is a stronger test of taste because the ratings came from people. It still scores only films they chose to rate, and it uses Dossier’s bundled BestSimilar descriptions rather than the live TMDB descriptions.

Comparison

Does Dossier beat simpler choices?

All methods rank the same 60 hidden films for each viewer. The other-viewers method has extra ratings from outside that viewer’s history, so read it as a separate reference.

The “similarly reviewed films” column compares only a liked and disliked film whose public scores differ by at most 0.5 out of 10. It makes public reputation less useful and asks whether the ranking can find a personal preference. Higher remains better; 50% is chance.

Change of mind

Does contrary evidence change a wrong claim?

The trial starts with five liked films from one genre. It checks for an active claim contradicted by hidden ratings, then adds up to eight opposing ratings from that viewer. Only trials with a qualifying wrong claim count in the correction result. Dossier’s internal strength score reflects its own evidence weighting; it is not a measured chance that the claim is correct.

Of the 26 successful corrections, 24 dropped the claim and 0 made it more specific. Dropping an incorrect claim is useful, but it does not establish that Dossier discovered the viewer’s more precise preference. These trials deliberately choose wrong claims; their correction rate does not measure how often all Dossier claims are correct.

Rating questions

Do Dossier’s questions teach it more?

Both sessions start with the same five ratings. One then rates films Dossier asks about; the other rates randomly chosen films from the more popular three quarters of the training pool. Positive differences favour Dossier’s questions. Dossier supplied an eligible film for 35.0 of the next 35 ratings per session on average; other slots fell back to the fixed rating order.

Ratings shownDossier’s questionsRandom reasonable questionsDifferenceMiddle 80% of paired differences
558.4%58.4%+0.0 points+0.0 points to +0.0 points
1061.5%60.1%+1.4 points−14.0 points to +13.2 points
2061.7%61.9%−0.2 points−17.8 points to +15.1 points
4062.1%63.2%−1.1 points−16.9 points to +15.9 points

Across viewers, the 95% uncertainty range for the 20-rating benefit is −3.8 points to +3.3 points. A range crossing zero does not establish that Dossier’s questions help.

Check the test

Does bad evidence hurt?

Each damaged session starts from the same 20 training films as its intact session. Negative changes mean the damaged ratings made film ordering worse. “Almost unchanged or better” means a drop under one point or an increase.

DamageAverage score changeAt least five points worseAlmost unchanged or betterDoes the check work?
Reverse half the ratings−5.4 points17 of 3110 of 31Average drop exceeds three points
Shuffle ratings among films−10.3 points18 of 3110 of 31Average drop exceeds three points
Remove the strongest ratings−5.5 points16 of 3112 of 31Average drop exceeds three points
Turn up to five likes into dislikes−2.7 points10 of 3117 of 31Expected drop not established
Give only five ratings−2.0 points13 of 3118 of 31Expected drop not established

2 checks did not reach the expected three-point average drop: Turn up to five likes into dislikes; Give only five ratings. Keep these flagged when interpreting learning gains.

There is a measurable reason for the weak aggregate drops. In the 11 intact sessions scoring over 65%, injected contradictions changed the score by −10.1 points; cutting to five ratings changed it by −8.0 points. In the 20 lower-scoring intact sessions, the changes were +1.4 points and +1.3 points. Damaging a session that already learns poorly can therefore improve its ranking. This explains part of the result; it does not clear the flagged checks.

Clues to the failure

4 of the 20 training ratings were neutral after conversion. 3 liked/disliked film pairs look almost identical in Dossier’s film-style representation. These similarity scores describe Dossier’s film representation and can miss differences viewers care about.

  • Liked Playing by Heart, disliked While You Were Sleeping; Dossier’s style similarity is 96.7%.
  • Liked Pitch Perfect, disliked While You Were Sleeping; Dossier’s style similarity is 96.5%.
  • Liked Sideways, disliked While You Were Sleeping; Dossier’s style similarity is 95.1%.

These claims also miss exceptions in the hidden ratings. This points to broad claims or the film representation as possible contributors:

  • Dossier thinks this viewer likes films tagged “Sentimental”: 3 of 6 matching hidden films contradict it. Examples: Ed Wood (2/5), While You Were Sleeping (2/5), Forever Young (2.5/5).
  • Dossier thinks this viewer likes darker films: 8 of 20 matching hidden films contradict it. Examples: Mission: Impossible (2/5), Jaws (2/5), Face/Off (2.5/5), RoboCop (2.5/5), Troy (2.5/5).
  • Dossier thinks this viewer likes complex plots: 8 of 16 matching hidden films contradict it. Examples: Mission: Impossible (2/5), Face/Off (2.5/5), RoboCop (2.5/5), Forever Young (2.5/5), Saw (0.5/5).

The downloaded data includes all 60 hidden ratings. These clues show associations; they do not establish which part of the code caused the errors.

Scope and source

What these results can and cannot tell us

Ratings: A frozen 2018 snapshot of the MovieLens small dataset from GroupLens. The dataset README explains the source and use conditions. These are anonymous people’s recorded ratings. We include all 31 viewers with at least 150 matched ratings, 40 clear likes, and 40 clear dislikes. Their ratings span past years and may include changes in taste. The source is a development dataset; we pin its archive checksum for repeatable internal comparisons. This report does not imply GroupLens endorsement.

Film details: Dossier’s bundled BestSimilar film records. We matched MovieLens entries by normalized title and exact year. We excluded ambiguous matches and translated genre names to Dossier’s vocabulary. The resulting 1736 films have real titles, genres, descriptions, themes, public ratings, and popularity; the records lack director and series fields.

Hidden answers: Each viewer has 60 hidden ratings. The CLI receives only chosen training ratings and public film details. We map 4 or more stars to a clear like, 2.5 or fewer to a clear dislike, and 3–3.5 to neutral. The same viewer never rates a held-out film during training.

Limit: MovieLens viewers chose which films to rate. The held-out set therefore represents their rated films, not a random sample of all films. Our title matching covers only part of MovieLens, and the missing director and series details may limit what Dossier can learn. Use this to compare Dossier versions on the same cohort, not to predict the experience of every user.

Use conditions: MovieLens permits research use and redistribution under its stated conditions. Acknowledge GroupLens; do not imply endorsement. Commercial use requires its permission.

Repeatability checked: Two complete runs matched in every result field. Each run included 124 learning sessions, 62 paired question tests, 31 claim trials, and 186 intact or damaged sessions.
